doc.title: Tom Malone interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 3, 2023

title: Horn voicings: trumpet, tenor, trombone and unison
summary: Malone explains standard R&B voicings on an F7 chord and why unison is best for small horn sections.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: When you were writing for them and for bands with horns, a lot of times like let’s say you had trumpet, tenor and trombone. What — is your voicing you’d think, well obviously the trumpet’s going to be on the top and the tenor’s going to go in the middle and the trombone’s on the bottom. Is that true?
Or do you mess with that?

Well the mess — no I basically followed the cue of standard rhythm & blues voicings. If you have an F7 chord you have the trumpet on the F at the top, a sixth below you have the tenor on the A, and you have the trombone on the E flat below that. And that’s the standard voicing. And when you have a small horn section the best voicing is unison. And when I say unison it’s really the trumpet and then the tenor and the trombone one octave lower. That’s what I call a unison.
And if you have a baritone sax he’s another octave down there. And in the case of that F7 chord you know the baritone sax has a low F.

And the trumpet could have — depending on the, you know whether you want the horns to stick out or not — the trumpet could have the C instead of the F, especially if you have a baritone sax covering the F on the bottom.
So it could be from the top down C-A-E flat, and then F down on the bottom.
